analysis.one_liner: Requires rail and air carriers to reinstate senior strikers when a strike ends.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died in a subcommittee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Railway Labor Act, railroad and airline employers must take back employees at the end of a strike. This bill would have made it an unfair labor practice for a carrier to keep employees hired or brought back during the strike while refusing to reinstate more-senior employees who had walked out. In practice, it protected striking workers with seniority from being permanently replaced by people who crossed the picket line.
analysis.who_benefits: Railroad and airline employees who go on strike, especially those with substantial seniority, would gain a guarantee that their jobs come back to them when the strike ends rather than going to strikebreakers the employer prefers to keep.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful, at the conclusion of a strike, for a carrier to fail to reinstate any employee with greater seniority rights than employees who returned to work during the strike and whom the employer wants to keep. [S2] [S3]

Adds this reinstatement duty to the Railway Labor Act's existing requirement that carriers not dismiss employees for union activity, so senior strikers get the law's unfair-labor-practice protections. [S3]
Applies to strikes beginning on or after January 1, 1990, giving carriers notice of the new rule. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Railroad and airline carriers would bear the cost: they could no longer retain strikebreakers ahead of senior employees returning from a strike, reducing their leverage in labor disputes and complicating staffing after a strike.

drawbacks.text: Carriers argue the bill would tilt strike negotiations by forcing them to take back senior strikers even when they have already retrained or retained replacements, reducing employers' ability to keep operations running. This is the standard employer objection to anti-strikebreaker rules; it is the position the bill's text would impose, and the record contains no carrier testimony. [S3]
The protection applies only to employees with greater seniority rights than retained strikebreakers, so junior strikers could still be permanently replaced. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers covered, the benefit is direct and significant: seniority becomes real across a strike, instead of evaporating the moment someone crosses the picket line. The cost falls on carriers in the form of reduced strike leverage and post-strike staffing constraints, and the protection is deliberately narrow, covering only senior employees. It is a modest, targeted labor bill rather than a sweeping change.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 1989, sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, then referred to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended with no hearings, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Martin Russo introduced the bill on June 13, 1989, joined by Representative Miller of California. [S3] [S5]
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, the committee with jurisdiction over the Railway Labor Act. [S5]
On June 26, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 101st Congress. [S5]
The bill attracted 23 cosponsors, 22 Democrats and 1 Republican, but never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote in either chamber. [S4] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rail and airline carriers are better off: because the bill never advanced, they keep the ability to retain strikebreakers over senior employees returning from a strike, preserving their leverage in labor disputes. Striking workers with seniority gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Martin A. Russo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require reinstatement of senior strikers.

for.name: Rep. George Miller of California
for.what_they_did: Joined Russo in introducing the bill on the day it was filed.

for.name: 21 of 257 House Democrats and 1 of 175 House Republicans

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction; chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Transportation and Hazardous Materials Subcommittee on June 26, 1989, and took no further action: no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was nearly all Democratic (22 of 23 cosponsors, with one Republican), and no vote ever occurred, so the chamber as a whole never took a position.

industries.note: The bill would have barred carriers from keeping strikebreakers over senior employees returning from a strike, weakening employer leverage during railroad and airline strikes. Because it died, carriers keep that leverage.
The bill would have strengthened strikers' right to their jobs back, a core union goal under the Railway Labor Act. It died in subcommittee, so unions gained nothing.
